documents.title: Induction at Fort MacArthur
documents.summary: Arrival in Los Angeles, uniforms, shots, and the first lesson about volunteering for 'police work.'
documents.currentTranscription: I was inducted into the Army the 7th of October 1943 in Los Angeles, CA. I reported to Fort MacArthur on the 23rd of October 1943. We were given a quick rundown of Army routine and issued our uniforms, given short haircuts, and several shots were administered. Some recruits passed out when they saw the needle. Of course, there were stories circulated about big square needles. I can't recall what shots they were, but our arms were quite swollen for several days. They gave us a preview of getting up quickly in the early morning, by blowing a bugle. You were to be outside in formation in 10 minutes. Your name was called and you answered Present And Accounted For. The Sergeant asked those in line who would be interested in Police Work to take one step forward. Quite a few thinking that would be a good thing to be in. The Sergeant then said all others line up for breakfast and the Police volunteers would Police the area. After they finished they could go to breakfast. It was a lesson not to volunteer if you didn't know what it is.

documents.title: Basic Training at Camp Barkeley
documents.summary: The train ride to Texas, tar-paper barracks, inspections, and the daily grind of keeping the barracks clean.
documents.currentTranscription: After about a week, we were loaded on a train to go to Basic Training. None of us recruits had any idea where we were headed. We went north for a while, then we went over the Sierra Nevada Mts. It was a beautiful ride. After a two-day ride we disembarked at Abilene, Texas. We were taken by trucks to a camp called, Camp Barkeley. As we arrived we looked at our nest homes. They were Tar Paper Barracks. The floors were planks and had cracks between the boards. We were told that these barracks were to be clean at all times. Not knowing Texas weather, it didn't sound too hard to do. They showed us how the Army wanted us to keep our footlockers. Footlockers are where you keep your underwear, your socks, shaving gear, and all your personal effects. Your shoes were to shine like a new penny. The barracks were to be kept so clean that if the Captain inspected and in wiping with white gloves got them dirty, the whole Platoon would be restricted and no weekend passes would be issued. No one wanted to be guilty of restricting all. There was a lot of soap and water used for Q'ing (cleaning) the barracks. After cleaning, then you hoped that the wind wouldn't blow, as the sand would blow up through the cracks in the floor. The inspection would happen after breakfast. They have a saying in Texas, "if you don't like the weather wait 5 minutes and it will change," this was so true.

documents.title: Live-Fire Training
documents.summary: Field drills, trench crawls under live ammunition, and the memory of a recruit carried off the range.
documents.currentTranscription: Basic Training lasted for 12 weeks. We had quite a lot of class work - learning map reading, compass training, Army etiquette (Yes Sir - No Sir), proper way to salute a superior, basic first aid, etc. We were assigned specific chores, working KP (Kitchen Patrol), Guard Duty. Also, we did daily marches with Galoshes. We made marches with full backpacks. We carried half a tent in our backpack and at night you pitched tent with another fellow, and you both have your tent halves. We also did night problems where you would be in a trench and you had to come out of the trench and creep and crawl across a field and they would fire live ammunition over the top of you. You learned soon how to keep down. It was a rainy night when we did this; the trench had about a foot of water in it, so it was real messy to creep and crawl. There was a young fellow who said He Couldn't Do This. He was told He Had To Do It so "get with it." Well, no sooner than he got out of the trench, he had an Epileptic Fit. They had to stop the guns and get a litter and carried him off the range. We never saw him again, so I guess he received a Medical Discharge.

documents.title: Medical Training at O'Reilly
documents.summary: Aptitude testing, transfer to Springfield, and specialized hospital training in bandaging and ward work.
documents.currentTranscription:
We had to take an Equivalency Test so they could reassign you to Officers Training or Medical Training at an Army Hospital. I scored 115 points and was given a choice of doing either training. I was getting a little Army smart and chose the medical training. While in basic training I took up smoking as each hour they would take a five-minute break and would say, "All light up that wants to." I thought why not join with everyone as they all seemed to enjoy the break. This bad habit lasted about 45 years and became so very hard to stop.

Finally the day arrived and I was called to go to Springfield, MO, to O'Reilly General Hospital. We were assigned to nice white barracks there, so much nicer than the Tar Paper ones in Camp Barkeley. We were told that we would go to classes and also work in the Wards at the hospital. I did good in all the classes except Ceph in Materia Medica. This involved the use of mathematics, where you also had to know about grams, and also problems that needed a Chemistry background. I never took Chemistry in High school. I was exceptionally good at bandaging, and after the class graduated and was to be assigned as a Unit, I and another fellow didn't get assigned, as they wanted us to stay a little longer and I was to teach field bandaging. I can't remember what Paul Wiehe was to teach.

documents.title: Back Across the Country
documents.summary: Reassignment from Missouri to Camp Beale and then back to Oklahoma to form the 135th Evacuation Hospital.
documents.currentTranscription: I stayed at O'Reilly another month and a half. Then I was sent back to Barkeley for reassignment. I was then reunited with a fellow from San Diego, his name was Sweeney. He had been a Pharmaceutical Salesman in civilian life. In Basic Training he had suffered a groin rupture and was just recovering as I returned to Barkeley. I was soon on another train headed West. I was on my way to Camp Beale in California. It was located near Marysville, CA. This was what they called a POC which meant you were going overseas. After a short time there, assignments were being made. They called 99 of us as a unit and instead of going overseas, we were to be sent back to Camp Gruber in Oklahoma to form a Field Evacuation Hospital.

documents.title: Unit Formation and the Blindfold Test
documents.summary: Additional classes at Camp Gruber, frustration with the cadre, and the start of the blindfold bandaging confrontation.
documents.currentTranscription: We again had to attend more classes and become a cohesive unit. We became the 135th Evacuation Hospital. The Cadre in our unit was a bunch of Infantry rejects; they all had stripes on their uniforms. After all the training some of us had, there was no way to upgrade our ranks and earn more pay. The worst part was, they were to do all the teaching. I fell asleep in a class on bandaging, and the Sergeant had a fellow next to me wake me up. He said, "I suppose you know all about this subject." I said "Yes Sir, and could do that without a bandage, blindfolded." Without what, he had me come up front, blindfold me, and said "Go ahead." I did the bandage, and after class I ran to report him to the Captain's office.

documents.title: Transfer to the Motor Pool
documents.summary: The confrontation ends with a meeting in the captain's office and a transfer that changes his role in the unit.
documents.currentTranscription: The First Sergeant wasn't going to let me talk to the Captain, as he was a friend of the fellow teaching the class. Well, in the meantime the class instructor came in, and there was some loud exclamation made. The Captain came to the door to see what was happening. He told the First Sergeant to cool down, and he asked me to come into his office. I explained what happened and I told him I would like a transfer to another unit. He said he couldn't do that but I could transfer to the Motor Pool if I wanted, and I wouldn't have to attend any more classes. I readily agreed and I really liked Sergeant Garcia who ran the Motor Pool. He made me the Motor Pool Dispatcher.

documents.title: Convoy Departure from New York
documents.summary: The unit stages through Fort Dix, boards ship in New York, and joins a 99-boat convoy bound for Europe.
documents.currentTranscription: Soon after we were on the train and we found our destination to be Fort Dix near New Brunswick, New Jersey. After a couple of days there we were taken to New York and boarded a ship headed for Europe. We didn't know it but we were in a 99-boat Convoy headed for France, finally going to the War Zone. We departed New York the 23rd of March. It was interesting looking either direction to see boats, all in a row, as far as you could see. Each day we practiced drills, in case there would be an emergency. We were to come to the deck for instructions. The ship was three decks deep in the vessel. Many people on the boat were sea sick. It was estimated by sick bay about 60% of personnel were up chucking.

documents.title: Collision at Sea
documents.summary: A nighttime crash in fog nearly turns catastrophic when another ship carrying high-octane gasoline crosses the convoy's path.
documents.currentTranscription: On about the 5th night around 10 pm I was laying on my bunk when there was a grinding sound. The boat kind of lurched. I thought like we had struck a sand bar and it was moving back and forth trying to dislodge itself. Then the emergency bells and lights came on and we were to go to the deck. Several fellows completely lost it. A big fellow from Oklahoma came running and flailing his arms. We ran over quite a few people and really messed up the evacuation drill. I and a fellow named Dean decided there was no way to try to get out, and that we would just wait and go out when things quieted down. What happened was not a torpedo, but the night was quite foggy, and the boat to our right mistook a blinker signal and turned, and came right in front of us. We hit them right in the middle of their boat. It hit them right in the Crew Quarters. We heard it killed seven of their crew. The scraping sound we heard was our boat trying to dislodge from them. Their cargo was Hi-Octane Gasoline. If we had hit them 10 ft either way we all would have been blown out of the water. The next morning the Captain said we did so good in the emergency drill that we wouldn't have to practice anymore. I figured the drill was a complete flop, and that we were so fortunate to be alive.

documents.title: From Southampton to Germany
documents.summary: Repair stop in England, Channel crossing, Camp Lucky Strike, and the rapid overland push through Aachen and Cologne to Hamborn.
documents.currentTranscription: Our ship was to go to Southampton, England, for repairs. We arrived in Southampton April 6 and was transferred to an English (Luny Boat) to go across the English Channel to France. We landed on the coast near Normandy Beach. We were assigned to Camp Lucky Strike, a Tent Camp, near Rouen, France. We never got our tents put up then we were told to pack up, and that we were now in the Second Army and that we were going to catch up to Patton's Army on his drive through France and into Germany. We went through the Maginot Line and into Germany through Aachen. The City of Aachen was a completely bombed out place. I don't believe that a single building downtown had four outside walls standing. We hurried through as we were trying to catch Patton. We passed a number of villages with no sign of warfare. Finally we reached Cologne, only to see it completely devastated. At this point we received orders to go to a town called Hambourne and set up our Hospital there. We arrived there and took over their hospital and all of the houses adjacent to the hospital to house our troops.

documents.summary: The motor pool settles into a large garage while troops barter food and candy for schnapps and small goods.
documents.currentTranscription: The Motor Pool took over a large garage and had a lot of room for our vehicles. We all learned a few words in German. We would exchange food and candy bars for schnapps. Schnapps is a very fine white wine. We also were able to trade for things like cameras, binoculars, etc.

documents.title: Supply Run to Paris
documents.summary: Driving Lt. Intrater on depot business leads to a stop in Paris and a visit to a subterranean wine cellar.
documents.currentTranscription: While in Hambourne, the Supply Lieutenant, Lt. Intrater was going to make a trip to several Supply Depots. Being I was the Motor Pool Dispatcher, I chose to drive him. A Sergeant from the Supply room was to go along. Our first stop was in Paris. We visited a wine cellar under the street. The wine bottles were stored on shelves that could be rotated. It took years for the wine to complete the circle in the aging process. After touring the wine cellar we came up into a large foyer, and they had us sample the wine. It was a white or clear as water wine and was very good.

documents.title: Marseille and Redeployment
documents.summary: With the war ending in Europe, the unit shifts south toward Marseille and waits under orders that might have sent them to the Pacific.
documents.currentTranscription: When we got back to Hambourne, the War in Europe was coming to a close. Shortly after we were ordered to go to a Camp near Marseille. It was called an R & R Camp, and was in the desert. R & R really means Rest & Recuperation. I really think they wanted us close to a port so we could be sent to the Pacific Area. After several weeks we received orders to load on a ship going to the Orient for occupation duty. An Armistice brought the war in Europe to the end. Now the problem was to bring our servicemen home to be discharged. A point system was devised to send the men who had been in the European area the longest to be first to go home. It so happened that we had been first loaded in our boat, then it was decided to load the highest point men on our boat and to send this boat to the U.S.A. They decided to leave us as they didn't want to unload our equipment.

documents.title: North Atlantic Storm
documents.summary: The homebound voyage crosses rough northern waters and leaves a lasting memory of the sea's scale.
documents.currentTranscription: We left France on the 17th of August and for some reason after leaving the Mediterranean we went north to cross the Atlantic by the North Atlantic route. We ran into a big storm and I just want to say I never believed waves could be so large. I'm sure that waves were 50 or more feet in height. We were tossed about like a leaf by those huge waves. We were told to stay below but, I just had to have a look. One look is all I wanted so I never forget that ocean.

documents.title: Fort Dix and the Trip West
documents.summary: The ship reaches New York, the unit returns through Fort Dix, and the final rail journey to California drags on for a week.
documents.currentTranscription: We arrived in New York on Aug. 27, 1945. Again we were sent to Fort Dix in New Jersey. We spent some time there and finally put on a train to go to California. Due to heavy rail traffic we spent 7 days crossing good old U.S.A. We arrived at Fort MacArthur Feb. 28, 1946.
